1.o: The foundation of all religion being laid in our relation to God as our Creator, it was fit that the book of divine revelations which was intended to be the guide, support, and rule, of religion in the world, should begin, as it does, with a plain and full account of the creation of the world—in answer to that first enquiry of a good conscience, "Where is God my Maker?" (Job xxxv. 10).
1.u: We have three things in this chapter:—I. A general idea given us of the work of creation ver. 1, 2. II. A particular account of the several days' work, registered, as in a journal, distinctly and in order. The creation of the light the first day, ver. 3-5; of the firmament the second day, ver. 6-8; of the sea, the earth, and its fruits, the third day, ver. 9-13; of the lights of heaven the fourth day, ver. 14-19; of the fish and fowl the fifth day, ver. 20-23; of the beasts, ver. 24, 25; of man, ver. 26-28; and of food for both the sixth day, ver. 29, 30. III.
1.i: God creates the heavens and earth in six days, makes people in His image, and rests on the seventh day.
1.p: Lord, You made everything, and it was good. Thank You for making us in Your image. Amen.
1.l: Go outside today and look at something God made, and say thank you for it.
q: Everything God made was good, and you were made in His image. How should that change how you see yourself?

2.o: This chapter is an appendix to the history of the creation, more particularly explaining and enlarging upon that part of the history which relates immediately to man, the favourite of this lower world. We have in it, I. The institution and sanctification of the sabbath, which was made for man, to further his holiness and comfort (ver. 1-3). II. A more particular account of man's creation, as the centre and summary of the whole work (ver. 1-7). III.
2.i: God creates the heavens and earth in six days, makes people in His image, and rests on the seventh day.
2.p: Lord, You made everything, and it was good. Thank You for making us in Your image. Amen.
2.l: Go outside today and look at something God made, and say thank you for it.
q: Everything God made was good, and you were made in His image. How should that change how you see yourself?

3.o: The story of this chapter is perhaps as sad a story (all things considered) as any we have in all the Bible. In the foregoing chapters we have had the pleasant view of the holiness and happiness of our first parents, the grace and favour of God, and the peace and beauty of the whole creation, all good, very good; but here the scene is altered.
3.i: A serpent tempts Eve, Adam and Eve eat the forbidden fruit, hide from God, and leave the garden.
3.p: Lord, we hide when we fail. Call us out, forgive us, and clothe us with Your love. Amen.
3.l: If you have done something wrong, tell God and tell the person you hurt. Don't hide.
q: Adam and Eve hid from God. What do you hide, and what would it be like to come out?

4.o: In this chapter we have both the world and the church in a family, in a little family, in Adam's family, and a specimen given of the character and state of both in after-ages, nay, in all ages, to the end of time. As all mankind were represented in Adam, so that great distinction of mankind into saints and sinners, godly and wicked, the children of God and the children of the wicked one, was here represented in Cain and Abel, and an early instance is given of the enmity which was lately put between the seed of the…
4.i: Cain, angry that God accepts Abel's offering and not his, kills his brother and is sent away.
4.p: Lord, You see what is in our hearts. Help us to rule over anger and jealousy. Amen.
4.l: Next time you feel jealous or angry, stop, take a deep breath, and talk to God about it.
q: God warned Cain before he did wrong. What warnings has He given you?

5.o: This chapter is the only authentic history extant of the first age of the world from the creation to the flood, containing (according to the verity of the Hebrew text) 1656 years, as may easily be computed by the ages of the patriarchs, before they begat that son through whom the line went down to Noah. This is one of those which the apostle calls "endless genealogies" (1 Tim. i.
5.i: Genesis 5 is a list of ten names in a row, and one of them is a person who simply walked with God.
5.p: Lord, we want to walk with You, day by day, until our walk is done. Amen.
5.l: Take a short walk today and talk to God as you go, as if He were walking right beside you.
q: The list says and he died again and again, and then breaks for Enoch. What would it mean to be remembered as someone who walked with God?

6.o: The most remarkable thing we have upon record concerning the old world is the destruction of it by the universal deluge, the account of which commences in this chapter, wherein we have, I. The abounding iniquity of that wicked world, ver. 1-5, and ver. 11, 12. II. The righteous God's just resentment of that abounding iniquity, and his holy resolution to punish it, ver. 6, 7. III. The special favour of God to his servant Noah. 1. In the character given of him, ver. 8-10. 2.
6.i: Noah builds the ark, survives the flood, and offers thanks to God, who promises that the seasons will never stop.
6.p: Lord, You keep Your promises. Thank You for saving Noah and for keeping the world turning. Amen.
6.l: Take care of an animal today, or thank God for the animals in your life.
q: The invitation came before the flood. What invitation to safety are you putting off accepting?

7.o: In this chapter we have the performance of what was foretold in the foregoing chapter, both concerning the destruction of the old world and the salvation of Noah; for we may be sure that no word of God shall fall to the ground. There we left Noah busy about his ark, and full of care to get it finished in time, while the rest of his neighbours were laughing at him for his pains. Now here we see what was the end thereof, the end of his care and of their carelessness.
7.i: Noah builds the ark, survives the flood, and offers thanks to God, who promises that the seasons will never stop.
7.p: Lord, You keep Your promises. Thank You for saving Noah and for keeping the world turning. Amen.
7.l: Take care of an animal today, or thank God for the animals in your life.
q: The invitation came before the flood. What invitation to safety are you putting off accepting?

8.o: In the close of the foregoing chapter we left the world in ruins and the church in straits; but in this chapter we have the repair of the one and the enlargement of the other. Now the scene alters, and another face of things begins to be presented to us, and the brighter side of that cloud which there appeared so black and dark; for, though God contend long, he will not contend for ever, nor be always wrath. We have here, I.
8.i: Noah builds the ark, survives the flood, and offers thanks to God, who promises that the seasons will never stop.
8.p: Lord, You keep Your promises. Thank You for saving Noah and for keeping the world turning. Amen.
8.l: Take care of an animal today, or thank God for the animals in your life.
q: The invitation came before the flood. What invitation to safety are you putting off accepting?

9.o: Both the world and the church were now again reduced to a family, the family of Noah, of the affairs of which this chapter gives us an account, of which we are the more concerned to take cognizance because from this family we are all descendants. Here is, I. The covenant of providence settled with Noah and his sons, ver. 1-11. In this covenant, 1. God promises them to take care of their lives, so that, (1.) They should replenish the earth, ver. 1, 7.
9.i: God promises Noah never to flood the earth again and sets the rainbow in the clouds as a sign.
9.p: Lord, You keep Your promises. Thank You for the rainbow, and for Your faithful love. Amen.
9.l: The next time it rains and the sun comes out, look for a rainbow and say thank you to God.
q: God put His bow in the clouds as a sign of mercy. What reminds you that God keeps His promises?

10.o: This chapter shows more particularly what was said in general (ch. ix. 19), concerning the three sons of Noah, that "of them was the whole earth overspread;" and the fruit of that blessing (ch. ix. 1, 7), "replenish the earth." Is is the only certain account extant of the origin of nations; and yet perhaps there is no nation but that of the Jews that can be confident from which of these seventy fountains (for so many there are here) it derives its streams.

11.o: The old distinction between the sons of God and the sons of men (professors and profane) survived the flood, and now appeared again, when men began to multiply: according to this distinction we have, in this chapter, I. The dispersion of the sons of men at Babel (ver. 1-9), where we have, 1. Their presumptuous provoking design, which was to build a city and a tower, ver. 1-4. 2. The righteous judgment of God upon them in disappointing their design, by confounding their language, and so scattering them, ver. 5-9.
11.i: People build a city and tower to make a name for themselves, and God scatters them by confusing their language.
11.p: Lord, Your name is above every name. Keep us from pride, and bring us together in You. Amen.
11.l: Learn to say hello in a new language today, and talk to someone who speaks it.
q: The builders wanted to make a name for themselves. Whose name are you trying to make great?

12.o: The pedigree and family of Abram we had an account of in the foregoing chapter; here the Holy Ghost enters upon his story, and henceforward Abram and his seed are almost the only subject of the sacred history. In this chapter we have, I. God's call of Abram to the land of Canaan, ver. 1-3. II. Abram's obedience to this call, ver. 4, 5. III. His welcome to the land of Canaan, ver. 6-9. IV. His journey to Egypt, with an account of what happened to him there. Abram's flight and fault, ver. 10-13.
12.i: God calls Abram to leave his homeland and go to a land he has not seen, with the promise of a great nation.
12.p: Lord, You called Abram and he followed. Give us faith to take the next step when we cannot see the way. Amen.
12.l: Ask God today to show you one next step, and take it even if you cannot see the whole path.
q: God called Abram to leave before showing him where. What is God asking you to trust Him with?

13.o: In this chapter we have a further account concerning Abram. I. In general, of his condition and behaviour in the land of promise, which was now the land of his pilgrimage. 1. His removes, ver. 1, 3, 4, 18. 2. His riches, ver. 2. 3. His devotion, ver. 4, 18. II. A particular account of a quarrel that happened between him and Lot. 1. The unhappy occasion of their strife ver. 5, 6. 2. The parties concerned in the strife, with the aggravation of it, ver. 7. III.
13.i: Abram let his nephew Lot choose the best land, Lot chose the green plain near Sodom, and God promised the whole land to Abram.
13.p: Lord, You are enough. Make us generous like Abram, and keep us from choosing only by what we see. Amen.
13.l: Let someone else go first today, in line, in a game, or in a choice. See how it feels.
q: Abram gave up the best and kept the promise. Where are you grasping for the best when you could trust God?

14.o: We have four things in the story of this chapter. I. A war with the king of Sodom and his allies, ver. 1-11. II. The captivity of Lot in that war, ver. 12. III. Abram's rescue of Lot from that captivity, with the victory he obtained over the conquerors, ver. 13-16. IV. Abram's return from the expedition, (ver. 17), with an account of what passed, 1. Between him and the king of Salem, ver. 18-20. 2. Between him and the king of Sodom, ver. 21-24.
14.i: When Lot was captured in a war between kings, Abram gathered 318 men, attacked at night, and rescued him and everything that had been taken.
14.p: Lord, thank You for rescuing us. Make us people who run toward those in trouble. Amen.
14.l: If someone you know is in trouble, don't wait to be asked. Find a way to help them, even if it takes some effort.
q: Abram rescued the nephew who had chosen the best land and landed in trouble. Who needs rescuing from a choice you warned them about?

15.o: In this chapter we have a solemn treaty between God and Abram concerning a covenant that was to be established between them. In the former chapter we had Abram in the field with kings; here we find him in the mount with God; and, though there he looked great, yet, methinks, here he looks much greater: that honour have the great men of the world, but "this honour have all the saints." The covenant to be settled between God and Abram was a covenant of promises; accordingly, here is, I.
15.i: Childless and afraid, Abram brings his honest complaint to God and receives a night full of stars as his answer.
15.p: Lord, You are our shield and our reward. Help us to bring You our honest questions and to trust Your answers. Amen.
15.l: Look at the sky tonight, count what you can see, and tell God one thing you are trusting Him for.
q: Abram told God exactly how he felt, and God answered him with stars. What would you say to God tonight?

16.o: Hagar is the person mostly concerned in the story of this chapter, an obscure Egyptian woman, whose name and story we never should have heard of if Providence had not brought her into the family of Abram. Probably she was one of those maid-servants whom the king of Egypt, among other gifts, bestowed upon Abram, ch. xiv. 16. Concerning her, we have four things in this chapter:—I. Her marriage to Abram her master, ver. 1-3. II. Her misbehaviour towards Sarai her mistress, ver. 4-6. III.
16.i: A runaway servant is found in the desert by God, who sees her, hears her, and promises to care for her son.
16.p: Lord, You see and You hear. Help us to notice the people others overlook. Amen.
16.l: Notice someone who seems left out today, and go and say hello to them.
q: Hagar felt unseen and found that God saw her. Who around you needs to be seen?

17.o: This chapter contains articles of agreement covenanted and concluded upon between the great Jehovah, the Father of mercies, on the one part, and pious Abram, the father of the faithful, on the other part. Abram is therefore called "the friend of God," not only because he was the man of his counsel, but because he was the man of his covenant; both these secrets were with him. Mention was made of this covenant (ch. xv.
17.i: At ninety-nine, Abram receives a new name, a covenant, and the news that Sarah will have a son in a year.
17.p: Lord, You keep Your promises even when we laugh. Teach us to trust You and wait. Amen.
17.l: Find out what your own name means, and thank God that He knows you by name.
q: God gave Abraham a new name before the promise came true. What does it mean to live in a promise before you see it?

18.o: We have an account in this chapter of another interview between God and Abraham, probably within a few days after the former, as the reward of his cheerful obedience to the law of circumcision. Here is, I. The kind visit which God made him, and the kind entertainment which he gave to that visit, ver. 1-8. II. The matters discoursed of between them. 1. The purposes of God's love concerning Sarah, ver. 9-15. 2. The purposes of God's wrath concerning Sodom.
18.i: Three guests arrive at Abraham's tent in the heat of the day, and one of them brings news that makes Sarah laugh.
18.p: Lord, You come to us in unexpected ways. Make us generous hosts and trusting hearts. Amen.
18.l: Welcome someone today with something special: a drink, a snack, or a big smile.
q: Abraham gave far more than he first offered. When have you given more than you planned?

19.o: The contents of this chapter we have, 2 Pet. ii. 6-8, where we find that "God, turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah into ashes, condemned them with an overthrow, and delivered just Lot." It is the history of Sodom's ruin, and Lot's rescue from that ruin. We read (ch. xviii) of God's coming to take a view of the present state of Sodom, what its wickedness was, and what righteous persons there were in it: now here we have the result of that enquiry. I. It was found, upon trial, that Lot was very good (ver.
19.i: Angels pull Lot's family out of Sodom at dawn, and Abraham watches from the hills as the city falls.
19.p: Lord, You are patient with us when we hesitate. Lead us by the hand, and help us not to look back. Amen.
19.l: When someone you trust tells you to hurry or to stop, listen the first time.
q: The angels took Lot by the hand when he hesitated. When has God gently pulled you along?

20.o: We are here returning to the story of Abraham; yet that part of it which is here recorded is not to his honour. The fairest marbles have their flaws, and, while there are spots in the sun, we must not expect any thing spotless under it. The scripture, it should be remarked, is impartial in relating the blemishes even of its most celebrated characters. We have here, I. Abraham's sin in denying his wife, and Abimelech's sin thereupon in taking her, ver. 1, 2. II.
20.i: Genesis 20 repeats a failure from Abraham's past, and shows God protecting both his promise and a king who did not know Him.
20.p: Lord, You protected Sarah and Abimelech when Abraham did not trust You. Help us to tell the truth and to trust You with the results. Amen.
20.l: Tell the truth today even if you are a little afraid, and trust God to take care of you.
q: Abimelech, warned of God, rose early to obey. How quickly do you act on a warning?

21.o: In this chapter we have, I. Isaac, the child of promise born into Abraham's family, ver. 1-8. II. Ishmael, the son of the bondwoman, cast out of it, ver. 9-21. III. Abraham's league with his neighbour Abimelech, ver. 22-32. IV. His devotion to his God, ver. 33.
21.i: After waiting for twenty-five years, Abraham and Sarah finally hold the son God promised, and name him Isaac.
21.p: Lord, You keep every promise in Your time. Make our hearts glad as we wait. Amen.
21.l: Think of something you have been waiting for. Thank God for it in advance, and keep trusting.
q: Sarah's laugh changed from doubt to joy. What is God turning from doubt to joy in your life?

22.o: We have here the famous story of Abraham's offering up his son Isaac, that is, his offering to offer him, which is justly looked upon as one of the wonders of the church. Here is, I. The strange command which God gave to Abraham concerning it, ver. 1, 2. II. Abraham's strange obedience to this command, ver. 3-10. III. The strange issue of this trial. 1. The sacrificing of Isaac was countermanded, ver. 11, 12. 2. Another sacrifice was provided, ver. 13, 14. 3. The covenant was renewed with Abraham hereupon, ver.
22.i: God tested Abraham by asking him to offer his beloved son Isaac on Mount Moriah, and Abraham obeyed, telling his son that God would provide the lamb.
22.p: Lord, You provide what we cannot see. Teach us to trust You with what we love most. Amen.
22.l: Today, tell God something that is hard to give up, and ask for help trusting Him with it.
q: Abraham believed that God would provide, even when he could not see how. What do you need to trust God for?

23.o: Here is, I. Abraham a mourner for the death of Sarah, ver. 1, 2. II. Abraham a purchaser of a burying-place for Sarah. 1. The purchase humbly proposed by Abraham, ver. 3, 4. 2. Fairly treated of, and agreed to, with a great deal of mutual civility and respect, ver. 5-16. 3. The purchase-money paid, ver. 16. 4. The premises conveyed and secured to Abraham, ver. 17, 18, 20. 5. Sarah's funeral, ver. 19.
23.i: When Sarah dies, Abraham negotiates to buy a cave at Hebron, the first piece of the promised land that he owns.
23.p: Lord, You keep Your promises, even in grief. Comfort us when we lose those we love. Amen.
23.l: Say thank you to someone older in your family today, and ask them to tell you a story about someone they miss.
q: Abraham insisted on paying for what he could have had free. When is it right to refuse a gift?

24.o: Marriages and funerals are the changes of families, and the common news among the inhabitants of the villages. In the foregoing chapter we had Abraham burying his wife, here we have him marrying his son. These stories concerning his family, with their minute circumstances, are largely related, while the histories of the kingdoms of the world then in being, with their revolutions, are buried in silence; for the Lord knows those that are his.
24.i: Abraham sends his trusted servant to find a wife for Isaac, and the servant stops at a well and prays for a sign.
24.p: Lord, You hear even our smallest prayers. Show us Your will, and help us to wait for You. Amen.
24.l: Pray about a small, specific thing today, and then watch for how God answers.
q: The servant asked God for a very specific sign. What specific thing could you ask Him for today?

25.o: The sacred historian, in this chapter, I. Takes his leave of Abraham, with an account, 1. Of his children by another wife, ver. 1-4. 2. Of his last will and testament, ver. 5, 6. 3. Of his age, death, and burial, ver. 7-10. II. He takes his leave of Ishmael, with a short account, 1. Of his children, ver. 12-16. 2. Of his age and death, ver. 17, 18. III. He enters upon the history of Isaac. 1. His prosperity, ver. 11. 2. The conception and birth of his two sons, with the oracle of God concerning them, ver. 19-26. 3.
25.i: Abraham dies at 175, and his sons Isaac and Ishmael bury him beside Sarah in the cave at Machpelah.
25.p: Lord, thank You for the faith of Abraham. Make us people who pass on Your promises. Amen.
25.l: Thank someone in your family today for something they gave you, like a lesson, a story, or their time.
q: A funeral brought two brothers together. What might bring you together with someone you have grown apart from?

26.o: In this chapter we have, I. Isaac in adversity, by reason of a famine in the land, which, 1. Obliges him to change his quarters, ver. 1. But, 2. God visits him with direction and comfort, ver. 2-5. 3. He foolishly denies his wife, being in distress and is reproved for it by Abimelech, ver. 6-11. II. Isaac in prosperity, by the blessing of God upon him, ver. 12-14. And, 1. The Philistines were envious at him, ver. 14-17. 2. He continued industrious in his business, ver. 18-23. 3.
26.i: Isaac reopens his father's wells, moves on when the Philistines quarrel, and finds Room and then peace.
26.p: Lord, You give room to Your people. Teach us to be peacemakers and to trust You to provide. Amen.
26.l: Choose peace instead of an argument today, even if it means giving up something small.
q: Isaac kept moving until he found room. How do you handle a quarrel over something you need?

27.o: In this chapter we return to the typical story of the struggle between Esau and Jacob. Esau had profanely sold the birthright to Jacob; but Esau hopes he shall be never the poorer, nor Jacob the richer, for that bargain, while he preserves his interest in his father's affections, and so secures the blessing. Here therefore we find how he was justly punished for his contempt of the birthright (of which he foolishly deprived himself) with the loss of the blessing, of which Jacob fraudulently deprives him.
27.i: Jacob disguises himself as Esau and receives the blessing of his blind father Isaac.
27.p: Lord, You keep Your promises without our schemes. Help us to be honest and to wait for You. Amen.
27.l: If you have said something untrue today, tell the truth and say sorry.
q: Jacob got the blessing by deceit. Is there something good you are trying to get the wrong way?

28.o: We have here, I. Jacob parting with his parents, to go to Padan-aram; the charge his father gave him (ver. 1, 2), the blessing he sent him away with (ver. 3, 4), his obedience to the orders given him (ver. 5, 10), and the influence this had upon Esau, ver. 6-9. II. Jacob meeting with God, and his communion with him by the way. And there, 1. His vision of the ladder, ver. 11, 12. 2. The gracious promises God made him, ver. 13-15. 3. The impression this made upon him, ver. 16-19. 4.
28.i: Esau finds out the blessing is gone, and Jacob must flee to his uncle Laban in Haran.
28.p: Lord, You go with us even when we have made a mess. Lead us home, and heal our families. Amen.
28.l: If you are angry with someone, wait a day before you say anything, and then talk to God about it.
q: Jacob had to leave everything behind, partly because of his own mistake. How does God work with us after we have failed?

29.o: This chapter gives us an account of God's providences concerning Jacob, pursuant to the promises made to him in the foregoing chapter. I. How he was brought in safety to his journey's end, and directed to his relations there, who bade him welcome, ver. 1-14. II. How he was comfortably disposed of in marriage, ver. 15-30. III. How his family was built up in the birth of four sons, ver. 31-35.
29.i: Jacob reaches a well near Haran, where he meets Rachel and her father Laban welcomes him.
29.p: Lord, You lead travelers to the right place. Make us hospitable, and lead us home. Amen.
29.l: Do something hard for someone else today, without waiting for them to ask.
q: Give thanks for the small circumstances of a journey. What small thing went right today that you did not thank anyone for?

30.o: In this chapter we have an account of the increase, I. Of Jacob's family. Eight children more we find registered in this chapter; Dan and Naphtali by Bilhah, Rachel's maid, ver. 1-8. Gad and Asher by Zilpah, Leah's maid, ver. 9-13. Issachar, Zebulun, and Dinah, by Leah, ver. 14-21. And, last of all, Joseph, by Rachel, ver. 22-24. II. Of Jacob's estate. He makes a new bargain with Laban, ver. 25-34.
30.i: God sees unloved Leah and gives her sons, while Rachel waits for her own, and then Jacob asks to go home.
30.p: Lord, You see those who feel unloved. Help us to see them too, and to praise You as Leah did. Amen.
30.l: Be kind to someone today who seems left out, and let them know God sees them.
q: God noticed the person no one else did. Who is God asking you to notice?

31.o: Jacob was a very honest good man, a man of great devotion and integrity, yet he had more trouble and vexation than any of the patriarchs. He left his father's house in a fright, went to his uncle's in distress, very hard usage he met with there, and now is going back surrounded with fears. Here is, I. His resolution to return, ver. 1-16. II. His clandestine departure, ver. 17-21. III. Laban's pursuit of him in displeasure, ver. 22-25. IV. The hot words that passed between them, ver. 26-42. V.
31.i: After twenty years of working for Laban, Jacob left in secret, was chased, and made peace at a heap of stones that was named a witness.
31.p: Lord, You see what we cannot. Watch between us and those we love, and keep us true to our word. Amen.
31.l: Make a promise today you can keep, and write it on a piece of paper somewhere you will see it.
q: The heap stood as a witness between two men who did not trust each other. What reminders keep you honest?

32.o: We have here Jacob still upon his journey towards Canaan. Never did so many memorable things occur in any march as in this of Jacob's little family. By the way he meets, I. With good tidings from his God, ver. 1, 2. II. With bad tidings from his brother, to whom he sent a message to notify his return, ver. 3-6. In his distress, 1. He divides his company, ver. 7, 8. 2. He makes his prayer to God, ver. 9-12. 3. He sends a present to his brother, ver. 13-23. 4. He wrestles with the angel, ver. 24-32.
32.i: Angels meet Jacob at Mahanaim, and he prays for help as he nears his brother Esau.
32.p: Lord, You surround Your people with angels. When we are afraid, remind us of Your promises. Amen.
32.l: Pray today about something that scares you, and remind God of one of His promises.
q: Jacob saw angels and was still afraid. What do you do with your fear?

33.o: We read, in the former chapter, how Jacob had power with God, and prevailed; here we find what power he had with men too, and how his brother Esau was mollified, and, on a sudden, reconciled to him; for so it is written, Prov. xvi. 7, "When a man's ways please the Lord, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him." Here is, I. A very friendly meeting between Jacob and Esau, ver. 1-4. II. Their conference at their meeting, in which they vie with each other in civil and kind expressions. Their discourse is, 1.
33.i: Jacob fears Esau but is welcomed with a hug, and the brothers part in peace.
33.p: Lord, You soften hearts and mend families. Teach us to forgive and to say sorry. Amen.
33.l: Make the first move toward someone you've quarreled with, and say sorry or hello.
q: Esau welcomed a brother who had wronged him. Who needs your welcome today?

34.o: At this chapter begins the story of Jacob's afflictions in his children, which were very great, and are recorded to show, 1. The vanity of this world. That which is dearest to us may prove our greatest vexation, and we may meet with the greatest crosses in those things of which we said, "This same shall comfort us." 2. The common griefs of good people. Jacob's children were circumcised, were well taught, and prayed for, and had very good examples set them; yet some of them proved very untoward.

35.o: In this chapter we have three communions and three funerals. I. Three communions between God and Jacob. 1. God ordered Jacob to Beth-el; and, in obedience to that order, he purged his house of idols, and prepared for that journey, ver. 1-5. 2. Jacob built an altar at Beth-el, to the honour of God that had appeared to him, and in performance of his vow, ver. 6, 7. 3. God appeared to him again, and confirmed the change of his name and covenant with him (ver.
35.s: Get Rid of the Foreign Gods
35.i: On God's command Jacob had his household bury their foreign gods and earrings under an oak at Shechem and set out for Bethel, and God kept them safe.
35.p: Lord, we want You alone. Show us the little gods we carry, and give us courage to bury them. Amen.
35.l: Look around your room for anything that you love more than you love God. Put it away for a day.
q: Jacob's family had to bury their idols before they could worship. What might you need to put away?

36.o: In this chapter we have an account of the posterity of Esau, who, from him, were called Edomites, that Esau who sold his birthright, and lost his blessing, and was not loved of God as Jacob was. Here is a brief register kept of his family for some generations. 1. Because he was the son of Isaac, for whose sake this honour is put upon him. 2. Because the Edomites were neighbours to Israel, and their genealogy would be of use to give light to the following stories of what passed between them. 3.

37.o: At this chapter begins the story of Joseph, who, in every subsequent chapter but one to the end of this book, makes the greatest figure. He was Jacob's eldest son by his beloved wife Rachel, born, as many eminent men were, of a mother that had been long barren. His story is so remarkably divided between his humiliation and his exaltation that we cannot avoid seeing something of Christ in it, who was first humbled and then exalted, and, in many instances, so as to answer the type of Joseph.
37.i: Jacob shows his love for Joseph with a special robe, and his brothers' jealousy begins.
37.p: Lord, You love each of us fully. Help us to be fair, and to heal where we have hurt. Amen.
37.l: Treat each person in your family fairly today, and say something kind to the one who gets less attention.
q: Jacob's favoritism hurt the whole family. How can you love someone without making others feel less loved?

38.o: This chapter gives us an account of Judah and his family, and such an account it is that one would wonder that, of all Jacob's sons, our Lord should spring out of Judah, Heb. vii. 14. If we were to form a character of him by this story, we should not say, "Judah, thou art he whom thy brethren shall praise," ch. xlix. 8.

39.o: At this chapter we return to the story of Joseph. We have him here, I. A servant, a slave in Potiphar's house (ver. 1), and yet there greatly honoured and favoured, 1. By the providence of God, which made him, in effect, a master, ver. 2-6. 2. By the grace of God, which made him more than a conqueror over a strong temptation to uncleanness, ver. 7-12. II. We have him here a sufferer, falsely accused (ver. 13-18), imprisoned (ver.
39.i: Sold to an Egyptian officer, Joseph rises to run Potiphar's household because the Lord is with him.
39.p: Lord, You are with us wherever we go. Help us to work well and trust You in hard places. Amen.
39.l: Do your chores well today, even if no one asks. Work as if God is watching, because He is.
q: Joseph found God in a strange country. Where have you seen God in a place you did not choose?

40.o: In this chapter things are working, though slowly, towards Joseph's advancement. I. Two of Pharaoh's servants are committed to prison, and there to Joseph's care, and so become witnesses of his extraordinary conduct, ver. 1-4. II. They dreamed each of them a dream, which Joseph interpreted (ver. 5-19), and the event verified the interpretation (ver. 20-22), and so they became witnesses of his extraordinary skill. III. Joseph recommends his case to one of them, whose preferment he foresaw (ver.
40.i: In prison, Joseph interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker, and asks to be remembered.
40.p: Lord, You never forget us. Help us to keep doing right when we are forgotten. Amen.
40.l: Do your job well today even if no one is watching or thanking you.
q: Joseph did good work in a bad place and was forgotten. How do you keep going when no one notices?

41.o: Two things Providence is here bringing about:—I. The advancement of Joseph. II. The maintenance of Jacob and his family in a time of famine; for the eyes of the Lord run to and fro through the earth, and direct the affairs of the children of men for the benefit of those few whose hearts are upright with him. In order to these, we have here, 1. Pharaoh's dreams, ver. 1-8. 2. The recommendation of Joseph to him for an interpreter, ver. 9-13. 3.
41.i: Pharaoh dreams of fat and thin cows, and Joseph, summoned from prison, explains what they mean and how to prepare.
41.p: Lord, You know what is coming. Give us wisdom to prepare, and humility to give You the credit. Amen.
41.l: Save a little of something good today, like part of your snack or some of your time, for later.
q: Joseph gave credit to God and then gave practical advice. How do faith and planning go together in your life?

42.o: We had, in the foregoing chapter, the fulfilling of the dreams which Joseph had interpreted: in this and the following chapters we have the fulfilling of the dreams which Joseph himself had dreamed, that his father's family should do homage to him.
42.i: Famine drives Joseph's brothers to Egypt, where they bow before the brother they sold and do not recognize him.
42.p: Lord, You bring hidden things into the light. Give us honest hearts and the courage to say we are sorry. Amen.
42.l: Say sorry today for something you have been putting off.
q: The brothers finally spoke their guilt out loud. What do you need to say out loud to someone?

43.o: Here the story of Joseph's brethren is carried on, and very particularly related. I. Their melancholy parting with their father Jacob in Canaan, ver. 1-14. II. Their pleasant meeting with Joseph in Egypt, ver. 15, &c. For on this occasion nothing occurs there but what is agreeable and pleasant.
43.i: Joseph tests his brothers by hiding his silver cup in Benjamin's sack, to see what they will do.
43.p: Lord, give us the loyalty to stand with those who are in trouble. Amen.
43.l: Stick with a friend today who is in trouble, even when it would be easier to walk away.
q: The brothers could have left Benjamin and gone free. What would you have done?

44.o: Joseph, having entertained his brethren, dismissed them; but here we have them brought back in a greater fright than any they had been in yet. Observe, I. What method he took both to humble them further and also to try their affection to his brother Benjamin, by which he would be able to judge of the sincerity of their repentance for what they had done against himself, of which he was desirous to be satisfied before he manifested his reconciliation to them.
44.i: Joseph tests his brothers by hiding his silver cup in Benjamin's sack, to see what they will do.
44.p: Lord, give us the loyalty to stand with those who are in trouble. Amen.
44.l: Stick with a friend today who is in trouble, even when it would be easier to walk away.
q: The brothers could have left Benjamin and gone free. What would you have done?

45.o: It is a pity that this chapter and the foregoing should be parted, and read asunder. There we had Judah's intercession for Benjamin, with which, we may suppose, the rest of his brethren signified their concurrence; Joseph let him go on without interruption, heard all he had to say, and then answered it all in one word, "I am Joseph."
45.i: Joseph reveals himself to his brothers, forgives them, and tells them God sent him to Egypt to save lives.
45.p: Lord, You turn the harm others plan into good. Teach us to forgive as Joseph did. Amen.
45.l: Forgive someone today who hurt you, and tell them so out loud.
q: Joseph said God used what the brothers meant for harm. Where have you seen God do that?

46.o: Jacob is here removing to Egypt in his old age, forced thither by a famine, and invited thither by a son. Here, I. God sends him thither, ver. 1-4. II. All his family goes with him, ver. 5-27. III. Joseph bids him welcome, ver. 28-34.
46.s: Do Not Be Afraid to Go Down
46.i: At Beersheba, God appears to Jacob and tells him not to be afraid to go down to Egypt.
46.p: Lord, You go with us into places we have never been. Help us not to be afraid. Amen.
46.l: If you are afraid of something new, say out loud, God is with me.
q: God told Jacob not to be afraid before he took a big step. What step is ahead of you?

47.o: In this chapter we have instances, I. Of Joseph's kindness and affection to his relations, presenting his brethren first and then his father to Pharaoh (ver. 1-10), settling them in Goshen, and providing for them there (ver. 11, 12), and paying his respects to his father when he sent for him, ver. 27-31. II. Of Joseph's justice between prince and people in a very critical affair, selling Pharaoh's corn to his subjects with reasonable profits to Pharaoh, and yet without any wrong to them, ver. 13, &c.
47.i: Joseph rides out to meet his father Jacob in Goshen, and Jacob meets Pharaoh and blesses him.
47.p: Lord, You bring families back together. Thank You for the joy of being found. Amen.
47.l: Run to hug someone in your family today, and tell them how glad you are to see them.
q: Jacob called his life few and hard, but he blessed a king. What does that teach you about suffering and blessing?

48.o: The time drawing nigh that Israel must die, having, in the former chapter, given order about his burial, in this he takes leave of his grand-children by Joseph, and in the next of all his children. Thus Jacob's dying words are recorded, because he then spoke by a spirit of prophecy; Abraham's and Isaac's are not. God's gifts and graces shine forth much more in some saints than in others upon their death-beds. The Spirit, like the wind, blows where it listeth. In this chapter, I.
48.i: Jacob, nearly blind, crosses his hands to bless Joseph's younger son Ephraim first.
48.p: Lord, You choose in ways we do not expect. Thank You for blessing us. Amen.
48.l: Say something good about a younger sibling or friend today, and let them know you think they are special.
q: God chose the younger over the older again and again. What does that tell you about how God sees people?

49.o: This chapter is a prophecy; the likest to it we have yet met with was that of Noah, ch. ix. 25, &c. Jacob is here upon his death-bed, making his will. He put it off till now, because dying men's words are apt to make deep impressions, and to be remembered long: what he said here, he could not say when he would, but as the Spirit gave him utterance, who chose this time, that divine strength might be perfected in his weakness.
49.i: Jacob blesses his sons and asks to be buried at Machpelah, and Egypt and Canaan join in a great funeral procession.
49.p: Lord, You are the God of the living and the dead. Help us to leave a legacy of faith. Amen.
49.l: Tell a family member today one thing you love about them, before the time comes when you cannot.
q: How do you speak about the end of life to the people you love?

50.o: Here is, I. The preparation for Jacob's funeral, ver. 1-6. II. The funeral itself, ver. 7-14. III. The settling of a good understanding between Joseph and his brethren after the death of Jacob, ver. 15-21. IV. The age and death of Joseph, ver. 22-26. Thus the book of Genesis, which began with the origin of light and life, ends with nothing but death and darkness; so sad a change has sin made.
50.i: Jacob blesses his sons and asks to be buried at Machpelah, and Egypt and Canaan join in a great funeral procession.
50.p: Lord, You are the God of the living and the dead. Help us to leave a legacy of faith. Amen.
50.l: Tell a family member today one thing you love about them, before the time comes when you cannot.
q: How do you speak about the end of life to the people you love?
